newsitem.title: GERMANY: German farm chief seeks to slow beef, dairy reform.
newsitem.headline: German farm chief seeks to slow beef, dairy reform.

text.p: German farm union (DBV) president Constantin Freiherr Heereman at a news conference on Thursday defended the European Union milk quota system and warned against Commission attempts to move beef production away from intensive methods.
Heereman was clarifying the views of German farmers on the two issues ahead of a January 20 farm council and meetings focusing on dairy reform under the Dutch EU presidency in the first half of 1997.

"We advocate milk volume quotas in order to protect our dairy producers, but we also realise the current leasing out of milk allocations has to end," he told reporters during the "Green Week" farm fair.
DBV was committed to milk market reform, but within the framework of the quota system.
The Dutch are understood to want changes to the system to prepare for the next round of world farm trade talks in 1999, although the current milk regime only expires in 2000.
Heereman said Germany's mostly small dairy and livestock producers could not live with milk price cuts suggested by an independent report and circulated at EU level.
Similarly, small but efficient German livestock producers would be threatened by attempts to reduce beef output in order to bring supply in line with sharply lower demand.
The Commission, which is due to present proposals on beef soon, is understood to be considering changes that could include incentives for less intensive grass-fed herds.
"A new ideology in favour of extensive cattle farming is not the answer," Heereman said. "It would be better to bring the market back into balance."
